If a system fault or outage which makes it necessary for the system to quickly obtain additional emergency relief generating capacity occurs while the pumped storage project is operating in the pumping mode at full capacity, the pumping load can be instantly tripped. This action is equivalent to instantly increasing the system generating capacity by an amount equal to the megawatt capacity of the tripped pumping load. The pump-turbines may then be quickly stopped, reversed, and fully loaded in the generating mode of operation. The net result of both actions is to bring an emergency source of generation to the relief of the troubled system in a very short period of time, producing a total output equal to twice the installed capacity of the pumped storage units. The first portion, equal to the tripped pumping load, is available instantly, and the time required to reverse the units and change from full pumping load to full generating load varies with the design of the plant, but is generally within 10 minutes.
Data available on a 240-megawatt reversible unit shows it to be capable of changing from full-load in the generating mode to full load pumping in 10 minutes and 4 seconds. This example probably does not represent the shortest time in which this turn-around can be accomplished nor is it claimed to be a representative time, but it is impressive as well as attainable.
Pumped storage projects have long life, low*forced outage rates, and high reliability. Knowledge related to the operation of an integrated electric utility system and production cost studies reveal that the relative merit of the proposed project, as compared to possible alternative actions insofar as economic and total system fuel consumption are concerned, can only be determined by studying the project or alternatives as part of the total system. This is because, when considered as a part of the integrated system, the proposed new source of generation modifies the economical dispatch of other units operating in the system.
Generating plants which incorporate the ability to economically store energy for future use modify the operation of the integrated system in a completely different manner than do plants which do not include the energy storage facility.
